subject: Automotive & EVs
title: La Jamais Contente
description: A fast breakdown of La Jamais Contente for builders.

hook.text: In 1899, a bullet-shaped electric car became the first vehicle to break 60 mph.

buildup.text: Belgian racer Camille Jenatzy built La Jamais Contente—'The Never Satisfied'—from lightweight alloy.

discovery.text: It hit 65.79 mph, proving electric motors could produce serious speed, not just quiet comfort.

twist.text: The record stood for three years, but nobody followed up. Gasoline cars took the speed crown next.

climax.text: It took over a century for electric cars to reclaim that performance reputation.

punchline.text: The first speed record belonged to an EV.

quiz.question: What was La Jamais Contente?
options: The first car to break 60 mph

details.summary: La Jamais Contente became the first road vehicle to exceed 100 km/h in 1899, and it was fully electric, proving over a century ago that electric motors could outperform gasoline engines in pure speed.
details.whyItMatters: This milestone demonstrated electric vehicle superiority in the earliest days of motoring. The fact that an EV held the world speed record in 1899 shows how old and proven the electric concept truly is.
takeaways: It broke the 100 km/h barrier on April 29, 1899
The torpedo-shaped car was powered by two electric motors
Belgian driver Camille Jenatzy set the record near Paris

faq.question: How fast did La Jamais Contente actually go?
faq.answer: It reached 105.88 km/h, or about 65.79 mph. This was extraordinary for 1899 when most cars could barely manage 20 mph. The record stood until a steam car surpassed it in 1902.

faq.question: Why is a 125-year-old speed record relevant today?
faq.answer: It proves that electric motor performance was never the technological barrier. Battery energy storage was always the limitation. Modern battery advances are simply catching up to what electric motors could always deliver.
